# The Qur’an Examined

## Expanded research edition 0.2

20 September 2026. Draft for review.

# An invitation to examine

*Opening essay · Draft 0.1 · 16 September 2026*

You need not begin this book by believing that the Qur’an is divine. Begin with a passage. Attend to what it says, how it says it, and what changes when its expression changes. Then ask how much that observation supports.

That is a modest beginning for a large claim. The Qur’an does not merely invite admiration. It presents itself as revelation and issues a challenge to those who doubt it. In 2:23 the challenge concerns producing a comparable surah. In 17:88 the claim extends to the combined efforts of humans and jinn. These passages establish the claim we are investigating. They do not, simply by being quoted, settle its truth. [Qur’an 2:23](https://quran.com/2/23), [17:88](https://quran.com/17/88)

The argument therefore asks more of us than noticing that a text is unusual. Every substantial work differs from other works in some respects. An unusual expression can be clumsy; a familiar one can be excellent. Nor does excellence by itself tell us that its author is more than human. Human literature offers extraordinary achievements, and a serious argument for revelation must make room for that fact.

Four propositions must remain separate: this text is distinctive; this text achieves something exceptional; the achievement is beyond human productive capacity, including exceptional genius; and revelation explains its origin. Each requires its own reasons. Neither the third nor the fourth can be borrowed from the first two without further argument. A comparative study may inform the case while remaining unable to establish universal human incapacity on its own.

We will begin with a sentence in a prayer. An old man speaks of weakness in his bones and a head overtaken by gray hair. The language turns grayness into a blaze. A reader may notice the image immediately. A more careful reading asks what happens when the head itself becomes the grammatical subject of that blazing, and how the image belongs to the prayer around it. The first sample chapter examines that question through a classical account of arrangement and meaning.

Then we will move to a complete composition. Al-ʿAṣr contains an oath, a judgment of loss, and an exception that includes both personal action and mutual counsel. Its brevity makes its structure inspectable. It also makes it tempting to confuse a striking interpretation with an exhaustive one. We will resist that temptation by considering the range of readings offered by commentators and by distinguishing grammatical observation from a claim about its effect.

Readers who know Arabic will be able to inspect some of these judgments directly. Readers who do not will need more explanation. A transparent translation can expose part of the reasoning, but it cannot reproduce every relation of sound, grammar, and convention. The aim is neither to hide behind expertise nor to pretend expertise is unnecessary. We should identify which judgments can be checked from an explanation and which require independent linguistic review.

The book will sometimes ask you to compare a passage with a deliberately plain reformulation. Such an exercise is a lens. It helps isolate a particular choice. It is not an adequate contest between the Qur’an and the best that human authors can produce. A weak paraphrase loses because it is weak. The comparative investigation must therefore bring in accomplished human compositions and allow them to display their own strengths.

It must also allow the Qur’an to be recognizable. Readers familiar with it cannot simply forget what they are reading because an experiment removes the title. Familiarity, devotion, and literary competence can coexist, but they are different influences. Our studies will record recognition and background rather than promise a blindness they cannot deliver.

Numbers can help when the question is precise. We can count a specified kind of repetition. We can examine how a defined alteration changes readers’ comprehension. We can compare judgments across passages, readers, and reciters. But a number answers the question built into its definition. A count of repeated words is not a measure of wisdom. A classifier that recognizes Qur’anic style has learned to distinguish samples; it has not discovered revelation.

The first computational appendix is intentionally elementary. It documents the source text, its numbered units, and the rules used to count written tokens. Its purpose is to make the analysis reproducible and reveal assumptions that attractive numerical claims often conceal. It supplies no score of literary excellence.

The larger argument will depend on the relationships among several kinds of evidence. Literary analysis must demonstrate actual achievements. Comparative research must ask whether the achievements remain exceptional under fair conditions. Historical work must independently examine the circumstances relevant to composition and transmission. Philosophical reasoning must then explain why revelation accounts for the resulting evidence better than the strongest available alternatives.

An exceptional human author is one of those alternatives. So are accounts involving inherited forms, a religious and linguistic environment, oral performance, and processes of composition or transmission. Their adequacy must be evaluated rather than dismissed by definition. Revelation, in turn, must not function as an empty label for whatever a current model fails to explain. The case for it requires substantive reasons.

This is an affirmative investigation. It aims to articulate the strongest responsible case for revelation. That purpose does not require protecting every familiar argument. If a numerical claim depends on changing the counting rule after seeing the answer, it should lose its place. If a historical premise is weaker than commonly reported, the book should say so. If a literary interpretation survives serious alternatives, it should receive the weight it earns.

The reader’s task is not to admire on command. It is to follow the evidence far enough to judge what has been shown, what remains contestable, and what further inference is justified. Our first task is simpler still: to read one expression carefully.

# The Challenge

*Research draft dated 20 September 2026. Translations are original working renderings from the Arabic unless otherwise stated. Commentary passages have been inspected at the linked locations; the complete works and their manuscript histories have not been reviewed. Independent specialist review remains pending.*

An accusation can explain very little. To say that a speaker invented something identifies a possible origin, but it does not yet explain the achievement. What capacities would the invention require? Which resources would make it possible? What should other capable people be able to accomplish under comparable conditions?

The Qur’an repeatedly brings the accusation of fabrication into contact with a demand for production. If this discourse is something a human being has composed, its opponents are challenged to bring something comparable. The move deserves examination because it asks criticism to become more specific. Instead of merely assigning the text to a familiar category, the critic must confront what that assignment is supposed to explain.

This does not make the challenge self-proving. An exceptional human composer might accomplish something that other people cannot reproduce. Nor does an invitation to compete automatically supply an agreed method of judging the result. But these objections identify work the argument must do. They do not remove the question the challenge opens: what accounts for the particular achievement before us?

## What the text asks

In 2:23, the address begins with doubt about what has been sent down to God’s servant. Its central imperative is:

<div lang="ar" dir="rtl">
فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِنْ مِثْلِهِ
</div>

An initial working rendering is: **“Then bring a surah like it.”** The verse continues by inviting the addressees to call their *shuhadāʾ* apart from God, if they are truthful. Whether that word emphasizes witnesses, supporters, or those able to attest a competing composition requires explanation. Even the short rendering of the imperative leaves an interpretive question: what does “it” refer to? [CH-01: 2:23–24](https://quran.com/al-baqarah/23-24)

Al-Ṭabarī makes that question explicit. He records an interpretation referring the pronoun to the Qur’an and another referring it to Muhammad as a human being. He prefers the former, using the parallel demand in 10:38 to support his reading. His discussion also emphasizes that the challenge addresses people through their own Arabic language. It does not demand competence in a language foreign to them. Later in the same commentary, he records explanations of *shuhadāʾ* involving assistance and testimony. These are inspected features of his interpretation, not proof that every commentator understood the verse identically. [CH-06: al-Ṭabarī, commentary on 2:23, discussion of “a surah from its like” and “your witnesses”](https://quran.com/al-baqarah/23/tafsirs/ar-tafsir-al-tabari)

The next verse matters as much as the invitation. In a close working rendering, 2:24 says, “But if you do not, and you will not, then fear the Fire.” The verse proceeds to describe that fire and those for whom it is prepared. The challenge is therefore situated within religious warning. The book should neither suppress that setting to make the passage sound like a neutral competition nor treat its warning as a substitute for evidence addressed to a doubtful reader. [CH-01](https://quran.com/al-baqarah/23-24)

Other passages vary the terms of the demand. In 10:37, the Qur’an rejects an origin in fabrication apart from God and presents itself in relation to preceding revelation and the exposition of scripture. Verse 38 then confronts the allegation that the Messenger fabricated it: “Say: Then bring a surah like it, and call whomever you can apart from God, if you are truthful.” The immediate subject is the origin of a discourse that makes religious and epistemic claims. Pleasant sound alone would be an inadequate account of what is at issue. [CH-02: 10:37–38](https://quran.com/yunus/37-38)

In 11:13 the demand is for ten surahs, described as *muftarayāt*, invented or fabricated. Al-Qurṭubī explains the imperative against the opponents’ allegation: if they say the Messenger invented the discourse, let them produce its like as something invented according to their claim. This makes the invitation more pointed. A respondent cannot simply say that genuine revelation is unavailable to a human competitor; the verse challenges the account in which the discourse is fabricated. Verse 14 then directs its audience, upon the failure of a response, toward acknowledgment of divine knowledge and submission. The passage itself makes the inference theological. Whether a contemporary reader should accept that inference remains something to investigate. [CH-03: 11:13–14](https://quran.com/hud/13-14), [CH-07: al-Qurṭubī on 11:13](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/qortobi/sura11-aya13.html)

The scale expands in 17:88. In our working rendering: “Say: If humans and jinn gathered to bring the like of this Qur’an, they would not bring its like, even if they supported one another.” This is a claim extending beyond a particular unsuccessful individual. It includes cooperation and reaches beyond human beings. A literary experiment with recruited readers cannot test everything asserted here. It can examine evidence relevant to part of the claim. [CH-04: 17:88](https://quran.com/al-isra/88)

Finally, 52:33–34 again places the accusation of invention beside a demand: “Then let them bring a discourse like it, if they are truthful.” The Arabic noun here is *ḥadīth*, rendered “discourse,” rather than a specified number of surahs. Al-Qurṭubī explains it in relation to producing something resembling the Qur’an from their own resources. This verse should not be paraphrased as explicitly demanding a single sentence, a fixed word count, or precisely one surah. Those specifications are absent from its wording. [CH-05: 52:33–34](https://quran.com/at-tur/33-34), [CH-08: al-Qurṭubī on 52:34](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/qortobi/sura52-aya34.html)

These passages can be compared without inventing a timeline. Their order in the muṣḥaf is not itself a chronology of proclamation. A historical account in which the challenge moves through successive stages requires historical evidence and an account of disagreement about dating. For this chapter, the secure observation is that the received text contains these different formulations. Ibn Kathīr’s commentary on 2:23 also gathers several of them into a connected discussion, showing a classical practice of reading them together. [CH-09: Ibn Kathīr on 2:23](https://quran.ksu.edu.sa/tafseer/katheer/sura2-aya23.html)

## The difficulty within “like it”

The repeated word *mithl* makes comparison central. Yet “like” is always like in some respect. A handwritten copy resembles its source, but copying would not demonstrate an independent capacity to compose it. A sentence containing the same number of words might match its length while failing in meaning. Conversely, an accomplished passage need not share the same rhyme to perform comparable literary work.

We should resist two temptations. One makes resemblance so easy that any imitation of surface features counts as success. The other makes it so restrictive that nothing except the original could qualify. Both empty the challenge of its intellectual interest. A contest in which mere rhyme suffices scarcely examines the achievement. A contest in which every difference disqualifies the respondent cannot distinguish inimitability from identity.

The project’s proposed reading is therefore concerned with **comparable achievement**: the relationship among expression, intelligible meaning, communicative purpose, and composition. It is a proposal for investigating the challenge, not a claim that these verses contain a modern assessment manual. Its adequacy must itself be discussed with Arabic specialists and readers whose commitments differ.

Consider what this means in practice. A short surah may combine a compact argument, a memorable sequence of sounds, and an address that changes the listener’s position. A fair comparison would ask whether another complete composition accomplishes comparably demanding work, with comparable economy and control. It would also allow the alternative to achieve something through a different organization. The comparison must identify shared demands without pretending that all good writing pursues the same purpose.

The word “complete” is essential. A single impressive phrase can teach us to notice grammar and imagery. The demand for a surah brings arrangement and development into the inquiry. How do its parts depend on one another? Does an ending complete what the opening starts? Are repetition and transition functional? What would a proposed revision improve, and what might it damage? Such questions give the comparison substance before a final verdict is attempted.

There is no reason to settle these questions by counting rhetorical devices. More metaphor is not necessarily better than less metaphor. A powerful warning may depend on directness. A prayer may gain force through repetition. The question concerns what the language accomplishes in its setting and how the parts of that accomplishment interact.

## Why the challenge is intellectually serious

The invitation to seek assistance makes the Qur’anic claim unusually demanding. Its explanation cannot rest on one opponent’s lack of talent. On the reading advanced here, the challenge directs attention to a possible disparity between resources available to opponents and the capacity to produce a comparable composition. That is a reason to investigate the strongest alternatives, not merely the most easily dismissed ones.

The affirmative argument begins with this explanatory pressure. If careful examination disclosed a sustained conjunction of achievements, and if strong human comparisons repeatedly illuminated rather than dissolved that conjunction, the evidence could support further inquiry into revelation. The relevant question would be why the whole profile occurs together, at the scale and within the circumstances established by the evidence. No one admired feature would have to carry the conclusion alone.

For example, economy may ordinarily impose a cost on explicitness. A composition might remain clear while opening several contextually defensible implications. Sound patterning may impose pressure on word selection. A passage might sustain a sound pattern while choosing an expression whose grammar is particularly apt. These are possible interactions worth examining. They are not results already established for every surah, and a striking interaction may still be humanly achievable. The positive research task is to discover which accounts survive sustained comparison.

The strongest human explanation deserves equal specificity. It might appeal to exceptional linguistic ability, long engagement with oral discourse, religious imagination, revision, interaction with hearers, or processes of transmission. Those possibilities should be investigated in relation to historical evidence. Merely listing them does not establish that they occurred or explain the details of the text. Equally, difficulty documenting them does not by itself establish divine authorship.

The argument improves when each explanation is asked to account for the same evidence. A proponent should not appeal to the Qur’an’s precision when convenient and excuse every difficulty as inaccessible mystery. A critic should not treat “human genius” as an explanation requiring no account of capacities, circumstances, or textual effects. Both positions can become insulated from evidence. Neither needs to be.

## What would make an investigation fair?

Before assessing a proposed competitor, we should specify the passage, its communicative task, the relevant comparison, and the reasons for selecting it. Those choices should be visible before judgments arrive. Otherwise an evaluator can shift the criterion whenever a rival succeeds: praise clarity until a clearer rival appears, then praise ambiguity; praise brevity until a shorter rival appears, then insist on fullness.

Readers should distinguish an observable feature from an interpretation and an evaluation. A repeated grammatical form can be located. An account of its contribution requires argument. A judgment that the result excels requires standards and comparison. Agreement at the first level does not force agreement at the last, but it gives disagreement something more precise to concern itself with.

Mixed panels of competent readers could help reveal where judgments converge and where they depend on prior commitments. Anonymizing a text would sometimes be useful, but recognizable Qur’anic language creates an obvious limitation. Recognition must be measured or reported, not wished away. Such studies are proposed work for this project. No panel has certified the argument developed here.

What could weaken it? Persuasive evidence that central interpretations depend on arbitrary divisions would matter. So would strong alternative compositions judged comparable under standards announced beforehand. Historical evidence that substantially improves a human account would also matter. The appropriate response would be to revise the claim at the affected level, rather than declare every adverse result irrelevant.

Conversely, an unsuccessful entrant establishes only that this entrant, under these conditions and these criteria, did not succeed. A hundred unsuccessful entrants would still not constitute a deductive proof about every possible human composition. The universal claim of 17:88 is stronger than any finite contest result. A cumulative argument may draw on such evidence, but it must explain its inferential steps.

The invitation before us is substantial enough without shortcuts. The Qur’an places a demanding claim about its origin beside a demand that opponents address its achievement. Our task is to make that achievement inspectable, to give strong alternatives room to succeed, and to explain why the resulting evidence does or does not support revelation. The next step is therefore neither applause nor dismissal. It is to read closely enough that “like it” becomes a question we can discuss with reasons.

# The Distance Between Claims

*Research draft 0.2 · 20 September 2026. An original argument map for this project. AI-assisted drafting and source checks; independent philosophical and scholarly review pending.*

A reader can follow the analysis of a Qur’anic passage and remain unconvinced by the conclusion drawn from it. That response need not indicate inattentiveness, hostility, or a failure to appreciate Arabic. The reader may have accepted everything actually demonstrated and declined something that has not yet been demonstrated. If a discussion establishes how a sentence creates an effect, but ends by declaring that no human could have composed it, an important part of the argument is missing.

The missing part deserves a chapter of its own. The Qur’an's challenge is stronger than a request to acknowledge a pleasing style. In 2:23 it calls for a comparable surah, while 17:88 denies that humans and jinn together could produce its equivalent. These are claims about productive capacity, not merely reports of admiration. Establishing what the text claims is the beginning of inquiry into whether it is true. [D-01: Qur’an 2:23](https://quran.com/2/23), [D-02: Qur’an 17:88](https://quran.com/17/88)

This book aims to develop a case for revelation that can survive careful examination. It therefore needs to distinguish the steps by which evidence might support that conclusion. Making the steps visible strengthens the investigation: a reader can identify exactly where agreement ends, and a defender can supply the reason that is actually needed.

## Four questions, four kinds of work

The first question concerns distinctiveness. Can we identify a recognizable pattern of expression? A recurring form of address, a particular distribution of sounds, or an unusual combination of syntactic choices may distinguish one body of writing from another. Such an observation concerns identity or distribution. It does not yet tell us whether the pattern is an achievement. An awkward habit can be recognizable too.

The second question concerns excellence. What does a passage accomplish, and how well does it accomplish it? Here the discussion must move from counting features to explaining their function. Precision matters when a sentence must discriminate between meanings. Compression matters when a small amount of language carries relationships a reader can recover. A sound pattern matters differently in a warning, a prayer, and an exchange of voices. Evaluation needs reasons connected to the work the expression is doing.

The third question concerns the limits of human productive capacity. Even an exceptionally accomplished composition may be human. The best performance observed so far does not automatically lie beyond the class of human performances. To argue for inimitability in this stronger sense, we need an account of why the demonstrated achievement cannot be adequately attributed to human capacities, including extraordinary ones. Merely repeating that the achievement is extraordinary does not supply that account.

The fourth question concerns revelation. Suppose a familiar account of human composition proves inadequate. Why does revelation offer the right explanation? The answer must identify what revelation explains and why that explanation is preferable to the strongest available alternatives. An unexplained feature is not, by itself, a label naming its cause.

These questions can inform one another without becoming interchangeable. A close reading may provide evidence relevant to a comparison. A comparison may sharpen the challenge faced by an account of authorship. Historical evidence may affect which explanations are plausible. But the strength of one conclusion must not be silently transferred to another.

| Question | A defensible finding might say | What still needs an argument |
|---|---|---|
| Distinctiveness | This pattern separates the specified samples under these conditions. | Why the pattern is valuable. |
| Excellence | These choices serve specified purposes unusually well in the inspected comparison. | Whether human capacity is insufficient. |
| Inimitability | The relevant human-production account faces these specific unresolved difficulties. | Whether those difficulties establish universal incapacity. |
| Revelation | This account explains the supported evidence better under stated philosophical and historical premises. | Whether the premises and comparison of explanations withstand criticism. |

The third row deliberately stops short of announcing a proof. It describes the kind of intermediate result an investigation might responsibly reach while the stronger claim remains under examination. The table records proposed standards of reasoning, not findings already produced by this project.

## What a close reading earns

Consider the expression examined in [The Head Ablaze](https://inimitable-quran-project.workspace-114686.chatgpt.site/read/01-the-head-ablaze/). Making the head the grammatical subject of blazing contributes to a particular representation of grayness spreading through it. The argument is richer than noticing a decorative metaphor: it connects arrangement, image, and the purpose of a prayer. That analysis gives us something definite to discuss, correct, or extend.

Its immediate achievement is explanatory. It helps a reader understand why the construction matters. A further comparison with a competent alternative could ask whether that alternative preserves the same relationships, establishes different valuable relationships, or sacrifices one effect to gain another. Neither task requires dismissing the alternative as worthless. An alternative may be excellent and still fail to perform a particular combination of functions as well.

That possibility supplies a promising affirmative direction. Instead of demanding admiration for a single attractive feature, investigate the interaction of several demands. Does a composition remain precise while compressed? Does its sound pattern sustain its purpose without forcing an unsuitable expression? Does a local choice contribute to the larger movement? The interest lies in how the choices work together.

The investigation must nevertheless allow an alternative to organize its achievement differently. Otherwise the criteria will quietly become a requirement to reproduce the original's identity. If a proposed rival expresses a meaning clearly by another grammatical route, difference alone is not failure. The defender needs to explain which relevant achievement was lost, rather than merely showing that the wording changed.

This is why a paraphrase can be an excellent teaching device and a poor competitive opponent. A deliberately plain restatement helps isolate an effect. It does not represent the strongest human composition available. We should retain the teaching exercise and decline the inflated conclusion sometimes attached to it.

## From a sample to a universal claim

Imagine that a carefully selected comparison set has been examined and no item meets the agreed standard. This is a hypothetical example, not a result of the project. The finding would concern that set, those criteria, and that process of evaluation. Its significance would depend on whether the alternatives were strong, the sampling fair, and the judgments dependable.

The finding would not, simply by its logical form, establish that no possible human composition could ever meet the standard. The examined set and the space of possible compositions are different things. Enlarging the set may strengthen an empirical case, but changing the scope of the conclusion still requires a reason.

A defender might seek that reason in a theory of the relevant capacities, in independently supported historical circumstances, or in a larger argument about the text and its claim. Those are substantial avenues of inquiry. They cannot be replaced by an unqualified assertion that an exhaustive test has occurred when it has not.

The same discipline applies to historical nonresponse. An account claiming that capable opponents had compelling reasons to attempt a comparison, understood what was being demanded, and nevertheless failed would matter if established. Each component needs evidence: ability, motivation, opportunity, the nature of the demand, and the surviving record. Silence in a selected source does not automatically establish every component.

Nor is our inability to reproduce an achievement a complete account of human inability. A reader may be unable to compose a skilled poem, solve a mathematical problem, or perform a difficult piece of music. That limitation can motivate respect and investigation. It does not identify the upper boundary of the species. The Qur’anic claim deserves an argument proportionate to its scope.

## Giving revelation explanatory content

In a cumulative argument, an explanation is judged against the supported evidence and serious alternatives. Philosophers discuss this under inference to the best explanation, or abduction. The method does not make a conclusion logically inevitable merely because it is preferred to the candidates considered. Igor Douven's discussion also identifies a difficulty relevant here: an inquiry can overlook a better alternative and select only the best of its incomplete set. The account and its justification are themselves debated. [D-03: Douven, “Abduction,” introduction and §2](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/abduction/)

For this project, the practical response is to improve the alternatives. Exceptional human ability should be represented by more than the label “genius.” What capacities and processes would that account involve? What can an account of oral composition explain? Which linguistic resources were available, according to historical evidence? How might transmission bear on the textual state being analyzed? A satisfactory assessment must investigate these questions rather than use their unanswered status as an automatic victory.

Revelation also needs more content than “something humans did not do.” Within the Qur’an's own presentation, the communication has a speaker, an addressee, purposes, and a claim on human response. A theological account of its origin must explain why the observed literary achievements are intelligibly related to those purposes. It must also engage the historical and philosophical premises on which identifying the speaker depends. This chapter proposes that research task; it does not claim to have completed it.

The affirmative argument becomes more substantial when it connects an achieved literary function to the character of the communication claimed. A prayer can make dependence intelligible through its movement and imagery. A short surah can integrate a diagnosis of human loss with an account of mutual obligation. Showing such relationships gives the theological argument real material to explain. It still leaves open whether a human author could have achieved them, which is precisely why comparison and history remain necessary.

A reader might already accept revelation through other arguments or experiences. That broader conviction can shape the questions the reader brings to the text. It should not be represented as a conclusion independently established by an isolated linguistic observation. Keeping those sources of confidence distinct makes the public argument easier to examine without demanding that a believer suspend every prior commitment.

## What would weaken the case?

An investigation gains clarity when it states the kinds of correction it can accept. If a grammatical premise is wrong, the interpretation built on it must change. If a proposed effect disappears when competent readers inspect the context, its claimed stability needs reconsideration. If a strong comparison preserves the relevant achievements, the narrower comparative claim must be revised even if a reader's religious conviction remains intact.

Evidence of dependence also matters. Suppose several apparently separate judgments derive from the same commentator, or several apparent literary effects are consequences of one underlying choice. Listing them separately does not automatically create several independent reasons. A cumulative argument must explain the relationships among its supports, not merely increase the number of items on a page.

Disagreement can itself be informative. If readers share the grammatical analysis but differ in evaluation, the dispute concerns value or function rather than the presence of the feature. If they agree on exceptional accomplishment but disagree about origin, another demonstration of the same accomplishment may leave their actual dispute untouched. Locating that difference prevents the discussion from becoming an exchange of increasingly emphatic restatements.

The case this book seeks is consequently demanding but intelligible. Begin with achievements that can be explained in detail. Examine whether they persist beyond favored examples. Bring accomplished alternatives into the comparison. Establish the relevant historical premises independently. Then ask which account best explains what has survived those inquiries, while identifying the philosophical commitments the judgment requires.

This route allows an affirmative conclusion to be pursued without deciding every intermediate result in advance. It gives readers something more substantial than an instruction to admire, and defenders a clearer account of what their evidence must accomplish. The distance between the claims is not empty space. It is where much of the work of the book belongs.

## Sources and review status

The Qur’anic challenge passages were inspected in their digital Arabic presentation. No hosted English translation is quoted here. Douven's introduction and the discussion of candidate explanations in §2 were inspected; the chapter's proposed application to Qur’anic inimitability is this project's own argument, not his position on the Qur’an. The worked linguistic example relies on the separately documented close-reading chapter. No comparison experiment, historical survey of all responses, or proof of universal incapacity has been completed. See [the source ledger](https://inimitable-quran-project.workspace-114686.chatgpt.site/research/sources-distance.json).

# A History of the Question

*Research draft dated 20 September 2026. This chapter follows selected arguments, not a complete history of the tradition. Classical passages and the extent of modern-source inspection are identified below. Independent specialist review remains pending.*

Someone hears a passage of the Qur’an and is struck by it. A second listener asks what, exactly, has produced that response. A third accepts the explanation but asks why an accomplished human could not have produced the same effect. These are different questions. A serious history of inimitability must preserve their differences.

The classical writers considered here do more than repeat that the Qur’an is beautiful. They examine the relation between wording and meaning, the conditions of successful comparison, the significance of an unanswered challenge, and the location of the miracle itself. Their answers are not interchangeable. Some disagreements reach the heart of the argument: does inability arise from the composition’s intrinsic character, or could divine intervention prevent an otherwise possible response?

This chapter approaches that history as a set of arguments we can still learn to examine. Respect for a scholar does not require accepting every premise. Disagreement among scholars does not make their analyses worthless. It makes precision necessary: which claim is being defended, with what evidence, and against which alternative?

## Al-Rummānī: eloquence has to communicate

At the opening of *al-Nukat fī iʿjāz al-Qurʾān*, al-Rummānī lists several grounds of inimitability, including the absence of a successful response despite motivation, the challenge, *ṣarfa*, eloquence, and truthful reports of future events. His argument therefore cannot be reduced to a single aesthetic test. In his account of eloquence, merely making a meaning understood is insufficient. How the expression brings that meaning to the recipient matters. He then distinguishes rhetorical operations including concision, simile, metaphor, and the fitting together of sounds. [HIS-01: displayed pp. 75–76](https://usul.ai/t/nukat-fi-icjaz-quran)

His discussion of concision supplies a useful restraint. Brevity can communicate economically or omit what is needed; expansion can explain fruitfully or waste words. The right amount depends on the task. He also acknowledges the excellence of brief human sayings and argues that judgment of inimitability requires a sufficient extent of composition. A striking fragment is not the whole demonstration. [HIS-01: displayed pp. 78–79](https://usul.ai/t/nukat-fi-icjaz-quran)

The consequence for this project is practical. We cannot count short sentences and call the result superior eloquence. A warning, a narrative, and an account of contractual obligations may need different amounts of explanation. Compression that obscures a necessary distinction can be a failure. Repetition that keeps an important relation in view can serve a purpose. The analytical question is what a formulation allows its audience to understand, remember, or recognize in its particular situation.

This also changes the burden of comparison. If we praise the Qur’an for compression but criticize another work merely for being longer, we have selected a winner through the rule. We must explain why the additional words are unnecessary in that other work. If they develop character, clarify an obligation, or establish an expectation that later matters, their contribution deserves consideration.

Al-Rummānī’s categories can thus prompt investigation without becoming an automatic scoring system. Finding a metaphor identifies a possible mechanism. Explaining its contribution is a further task. Establishing that no human composition could accomplish something comparable is further still.

## Al-Khaṭṭābī: admiration needs an explanation

Al-Khaṭṭābī’s *Bayān iʿjāz al-Qurʾān* confronts an uncomfortable problem for defenders of literary inimitability. He reports explanations that refer to an expert’s recognition of exceptional eloquence but cannot adequately specify its cause. He finds that insufficient. The felt effect should lead to an investigation of what produces it. In the passage that follows, he describes Qur’anic discourse as combining qualities such as grandeur and sweetness that can pull expression in different directions. He regards their conjunction as part of its excellence. [HIS-02: displayed pp. 24–26](https://usul.ai/ar/t/bayan-icjaz-quran/6), [continuation](https://usul.ai/ar/t/bayan-icjaz-quran/8)

There is a generous way to understand the appeal to expertise. A skilled reader may recognize a difference before explaining it fully. The inability to give an immediate account does not prove that the difference is imaginary. Yet expertise becomes much more useful to another person when it can guide attention: listen to this transition, inspect this relation, consider what the alternative would make harder to perceive.

For the present book, the combination of qualities suggests a promising inquiry. Can a passage remain forceful while being easy to follow? Can it be compact while allowing several relevant implications? Can its sound support its meaning without making that meaning feel forced? These are our proposed questions, not a modern experiment already conducted by al-Khaṭṭābī.

They also suggest why a single excellence score would hide too much. One passage might gain emphasis at the cost of conversational ease. Another might achieve clarity through deliberate plainness. The interesting question is how a composition handles the demands it actually faces. To present integration as evidence, we must first describe those demands and show that the claimed qualities are present together.

An affirmative argument can draw strength from this inquiry. It offers a more substantial account of achievement than “I find it moving.” But we should not transform an attractive description into a universal claim before testing it across complete passages and serious alternatives.

## Where is the miracle?

The dispute over *ṣarfa* exposes a difference that a history should not conceal. In a form of the view discussed by al-Khaṭṭābī, people could otherwise produce a response, but God turns their intentions away from doing so. The extraordinary event lies in the prevention. This account appears in his presentation of competing explanations; reporting it is not the same as endorsing it. [HIS-02: displayed p. 22](https://usul.ai/ar/t/bayan-icjaz-quran/4)

Al-Bāqillānī objects that, if composition were within human capacity and only prevention stopped it, the prevention would be miraculous rather than the discourse itself. He also rejects the inference that a person who can produce a fine short expression must therefore be able to build an equally fine complete composition. His argument places substantial weight on the character of the composed text. [HIS-03: displayed pp. 29–31](https://islamweb.net/ar/library/content/240/3/فصل-في-بيان-وجه-الدلالة-على-أن-القرآن-معجز)

These positions make different demands on evidence. Consider a hypothetical passage of ordinary literary quality that nobody answers because of divine intervention. That would be compatible with a prevention account as just described. It would supply little support for the claim that the passage’s literary properties themselves exceed human capacity. Conversely, identifying an unusually integrated composition does not by itself demonstrate that someone was supernaturally prevented from responding.

One should therefore resist presenting every classical argument as a vote for the same modern formulation. Nor should a defender silently move to divine prevention whenever a textual comparison becomes difficult. A change in explanation is possible, but it must be acknowledged and defended with the evidence appropriate to it.

This chapter does not assign one uniform prevention doctrine to every scholar associated with the term. Its narrower point is enough: an argument about what people cannot compose differs from an argument about what they are prevented from composing. Keeping those claims distinct protects the affirmative case from becoming impossible to examine.

## Al-Bāqillānī: compare with accomplished poetry

Al-Bāqillānī also undertakes a demanding comparison. In *Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān*, he examines verses attributed to Imruʾ al-Qays rather than confining himself to an intentionally weak imitation. He acknowledges the claims made for the celebrated opening, then contests them through criticism of its wording, implications, and elaboration. For example, he challenges the utility of its accumulation of place names. These are his judgments, not independently established defects in the poem. [HIS-04: displayed pp. 160–166](https://www.islamweb.net/amp/ar/library/content/240/38/باب)

The encounter teaches two lessons that must remain together. A serious argument should face accomplished alternatives. A serious comparison should also allow those alternatives a capable defense. The fact that a major theologian found a poetic detail unnecessary does not settle what that detail contributes within the poem.

A defender of the poem could ask whether geographic particularity anchors memory, establishes a setting, or gives the speaker’s loss a recognizable location. That is a proposed counterreading requiring its own analysis. It cannot be rejected merely because the same details would be excessive in a different kind of discourse. By the same rule, the Qur’an should not be judged defective for declining to pursue the purposes of an elegy or an ode.

The question is not whether comparisons are possible. It is whether the criteria respect the works being compared. Where purposes overlap, a judgment can become specific: which expression makes a relevant distinction clearer, which transition prepares the next movement, which pattern helps a reader hold the argument together? Where purposes differ, we must say so before announcing a result.

This is a demanding standard for a favorable case, but an advantage for the reader. A conclusion becomes more persuasive when it survives an alternative’s best explanation. Merely collecting adverse judgments about other writing would leave the central uncertainty untouched.

## Al-Jurjānī: look at the relationships

The chapter “The Head Ablaze” develops one precise example from ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī’s *Dalāʾil al-iʿjāz*. In paragraphs 91–93, he argues that the merit of Qur’an 19:4 cannot be explained merely by naming its fire metaphor. The attribution of blazing to the head matters. Formulations that make gray hair the subject organize the image differently. He connects the Qur’anic construction with pervasive spread and also attends to its use of the definite noun. The relevant scanned pages are 100–102 in Maḥmūd Muḥammad Shākir’s third edition. [HIS-05: PDF pp. 142–144](https://archive.org/download/loga13/121.pdf#page=142)

This is an especially useful model of criticism because its explanation refers back to inspectable choices. A reader can understand the difference between a thing that blazes and a place in which blazing occurs, then ask how the distinction contributes to the prayer. Agreement about the grammatical contrast does not force agreement about the degree of excellence. It supplies a shared object of discussion.

The method also guards against treating rare vocabulary as the substance of greatness. Familiar words can enter into relationships that accomplish something particular. Conversely, unusual words can be ornamental without doing necessary work. A reading must show what the arrangement achieves.

We can extend this approach through carefully designed substitutions, provided we distinguish a teaching comparison from a competitive trial. An alternative intended to isolate one grammatical relationship is useful even if it is artistically inferior. It cannot then stand for the strongest human alternative. To investigate the larger claim, we need both controlled explanatory contrasts and complete compositions written to succeed on their own terms.

## Modern scholarship changes the questions we can ask

Modern work offers several routes into this inheritance. Lara Harb’s publisher-provided summary of her chapter on *naẓm* emphasizes discovery: sentence construction can lead a listener to infer contextual meanings through choices such as omission, word order, and definiteness. It connects this account with an aesthetic of wonder. The summary and bibliographic information were inspected for this draft, not the full chapter. This is a scholarly interpretation of a tradition, not a measured claim about every listener’s experience. [HIS-06: Harb, *Arabic Poetics*, chapter 5, pp. 203–251](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108780483.007)

Mustansir Mir’s chapter “The Structure of the Qur’an: The Inner Dynamic of the Sura” directs attention to a larger scale. Its abstract describes scholarship concerning forms, contextual effects, verbal correspondences, section lengths, and central themes. It examines readings of the surah as a connected composition. Again, the abstract was inspected, not the full chapter. [HIS-07: publisher abstract, pp. 362–373](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/34388/chapter/291611299)

For our inquiry, this move in scale is essential. We should investigate whether the relations visible in a phrase also contribute to the movement of a whole surah. A convincing structural proposal needs explicit connections and a reason for its boundaries. A diagram is a representation of a reading. It does not establish that reading merely by looking balanced.

Two further studies identify useful paths for subsequent close work. Muhammad Abdel Haleem’s 1992 article concerns grammatical shifts and their rhetorical purposes; Devin Stewart’s 1990 article concerns *sajʿ*, prosody, and structure. The institutional and journal records verify these publications. Their complete arguments have not been inspected for this chapter, so they are reading priorities rather than authorities enlisted to endorse its conclusion. [HIS-08: Abdel Haleem, article record](https://soas-repository.worktribe.com/output/411099), [HIS-09: Stewart, journal contents](https://www.jstor.org/stable/i393966)

These research directions invite two symmetrical cautions. An unexpected grammatical turn should not be condemned before its context is examined. It should not automatically be praised simply because we can invent a purpose for it. Similarly, identifying a shared literary technique does not decide whether its particular use is ordinary or exceptional. Classification, explanation, and evaluation remain separate tasks.

## What this history asks of us

The positions considered here leave us with a productive set of obligations. Explain what language communicates, investigate the combination of its qualities, distinguish different accounts of inability, defend comparative criteria, and trace local effects into complete compositions. These obligations are our synthesis of the selected debates. They are not a claim that every historical author adopted one common method.

A skeptical reader may ask whether all this analysis simply rationalizes a conclusion inherited in advance. That risk exists for this project and must be addressed through its conduct. Readers should be able to challenge an interpretation, improve a comparator, identify a neglected source, or show that a claimed effect disappears under a better explanation. A favorable thesis is not a license to dismiss such contributions.

The affirmative possibility also deserves to remain visible. If the Qur’an repeatedly integrates expression, meaning, and purpose under demanding comparisons, that would be evidence worth accounting for. What it ultimately supports depends on the strength of those comparisons and the historical and philosophical premises added to them. The present history does not supply that final inference. It gives us better questions with which to pursue it.

*Source note: al-Rummānī and al-Khaṭṭābī were consulted in digital Arabic transcriptions identifying the 1976 third edition of the collection edited by Muḥammad Khalaf Allāh and Muḥammad Zaghlūl Sallām. Displayed pagination is reported; those transcriptions have not been collated with scanned pages for this chapter. Al-Bāqillānī’s passages were inspected in an online transcription whose print edition remains to be confirmed. Al-Jurjānī’s bounded passage was checked against page images. None of these limited inspections is a claim to have read or critically edited the complete works.*

# The Head Ablaze

*Sample chapter. Research draft dated 16 September 2026. Arabic and translations require independent specialist review before a reviewed edition. Translations without an attributed translator are original working renderings.*

An old man is praying. Before he asks for what he needs, he describes what age has done to him. His strength is failing. His hair has whitened. Yet the sentence in which he speaks does something more particular than report those facts:

<div lang="ar" dir="rtl">
وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا
</div>

*Wa-shtaʿala al-raʾsu shayban.*

An image-preserving translation is: **“And the head has blazed with gray hair.”** The final word is pronounced *shaybā* when stopping on it. The Arabic is the middle clause of Qur’an 19:4. [C19-01: Arabic passage](https://quran.com/maryam/2-6)

The expression is unfamiliar enough in English to invite a second look. A head does not ordinarily blaze with grayness. Why describe aging through fire? Why make the head, rather than the hair, the subject? And what does this image contribute to a prayer?

These questions can be investigated before deciding whether the Qur’an is revelation. We need not pretend that the theological question is unimportant. It is the larger question of this book. But a reader should be able to inspect the evidence offered in its support. Calling a sentence miraculous cannot replace explaining how it works.

This chapter therefore begins with a small, examinable claim: the relationship between the grammar and the image contributes to a recognizable literary effect. Whether that effect is admirable is a further judgment. Whether it belongs to a sustained achievement beyond human productive capacity is further still.

## A sentence inside a prayer

The speaker is Zakariyyā, or Zechariah. Verses 19:2–3 introduce the account as a remembrance of divine mercy and describe his private calling upon his Lord. Verse 4 gives his words. In verses 5–6 he expresses concern about those who will follow him, describes his wife as unable to bear children, and asks for a successor who will inherit and be pleasing to God. The precise character of the inheritance is an exegetical question; nothing in the present argument requires settling it. [C19-01: 19:2–6](https://quran.com/maryam/2-6)

Here is verse 4 in ordinary vocalized Arabic spelling, with the additional signs of the displayed muṣḥaf omitted:

<div lang="ar" dir="rtl">
قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا وَلَمْ أَكُنْ بِدُعَائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا
</div>

> He said: “My Lord, my bones have weakened, and the head has blazed with gray hair. In calling upon You, my Lord, I have never been wretched.”

This working translation preserves the fire image while making one grammatical accommodation: Arabic has the singular *al-ʿaẓm*, “the bone,” where the translation uses “my bones.” Its final sentence deliberately stays close to the wording; the familiar sense of not having been disappointed in prayer is an interpretation supported by al-Ṭabarī’s commentary. [C19-02: morphology](https://corpus.quran.com/wordbyword.jsp?chapter=19&verse=4), [C19-04: commentary on 19:4](https://quran.com/maryam/4/tafsirs/ar-tafsir-al-tabari)

The verse can be read as moving from diminished bodily strength to visible aging and then to remembered confidence in God. That is the reading developed here, not a diagram supplied by the text. It has a basis readers can check: the order of the clauses, the physical descriptions, and the final statement about prayer. The apparent obstacle to Zakariyyā’s request and his reason for making it are brought together.

## What the grammar lets us see

The central clause has three written words. That count uses the ordinary spacing of the Arabic, including the prefixed conjunction within the first word; it is not a claim about a uniquely correct linguistic tokenization.

| Arabic element | Basic function | What the reader receives |
|---|---|---|
| وَاشْتَعَلَ | “And blazed”: conjunction plus a past-tense verb | A happening pictured through ignition or blazing |
| الرَّأْسُ | “The head”: nominative noun, grammatical subject of the verb | The head as the thing of which blazing is predicated |
| شَيْبًا | “Grayness” or “gray hair”: accusative indefinite noun | The respect in which the head has blazed |

The case and verb information can be checked in the Quranic Arabic Corpus. The interpretation of the last word as a specifying accusative, *tamyīz*, follows the grammatical analysis developed in the classical discussion below. The Corpus’s word-by-word page identifies its accusative case; that fact alone is not a complete analysis of its syntactic function. [C19-02](https://corpus.quran.com/wordbyword.jsp?chapter=19&verse=4)

On the *tamyīz* analysis, grayness specifies an otherwise surprising attribution: the head has blazed, in respect of gray hair. It is not an object that the head burns. Nor is “head” an agent deliberately performing an action. “Grammatical subject” describes its role in the sentence, not a claim about intention or physical causation.

This distinction matters because loose explanations can turn an intelligible construction into a false mystery. Arabic is not violating its grammar here. It is using a grammatical possibility to present a relationship in a particular way.

Al-Ṭabarī also preserves a useful complication. He reports disagreement over the accusative *shayban*: one analysis takes it as a verbal noun expressing the sense of becoming gray; another treats it as specification or explanation. The existence of this disagreement does not remove the head’s grammatical role. It does prevent us from presenting one account of the final accusative as the only analysis ever available. [C19-04](https://quran.com/maryam/4/tafsirs/ar-tafsir-al-tabari)

## Al-Jurjānī’s invitation to compare

The attribution of this example to ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī can be made precise. In *Dalāʾil al-iʿjāz*, paragraphs 91–93 of Maḥmūd Muḥammad Shākir’s edition, he argues that naming the metaphor does not adequately explain the expression’s merit. The construction matters: the verb is attributed to the head, with grayness following in specification. He contrasts this with formulations making gray hair the subject and explains the Qur’anic construction through the idea of pervasive spread. He also discusses the definite expression “the head,” whose possessor is understood from context. The passage is on printed pages 100–102 of the third edition, 1413 AH / 1992. These pages and the edition statement have been checked against scanned images. [C19-03: scan, PDF pages 142–144](https://archive.org/download/loga13/121.pdf#page=142)

His procedure gives the reader work to do. Keep something constant, alter something else, and inspect the consequence. It is a way to make a literary explanation answerable to the wording.

The following comparisons are **analytical alternatives, not Qur’anic text**. The two Arabic alternatives follow the constructions considered by al-Jurjānī; the English plain statement is a teaching paraphrase.

| Version | Analytical wording | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| Plain paraphrase | “My hair has turned gray.” | The condition is stated without the fire image. |
| Alternative A | اشْتَعَلَ شَيْبُ الرَّأْسِ (“The gray hair of the head blazed.”) | Gray hair becomes the grammatical subject. |
| Alternative B | اشْتَعَلَ الشَّيْبُ فِي الرَّأْسِ (“Gray hair blazed in the head.”) | The head is presented as the location. |

The instructional advantage is also the limitation. We can see that the alternatives organize attention differently. We cannot infer that the less vivid English paraphrase represents the best humanity can compose. A demonstration designed to isolate a feature is not a literary championship.

Nor should “pervasive spread” become an anatomical measurement. The expression presents aging through an encompassing image; it does not give a percentage of white hairs. A reader might accept the larger impression while declining to infer that literally every hair has whitened. The distinction keeps literary interpretation proportionate to what language can establish.

## Why the image belongs here

Consider an objection that a sympathetic reading should not brush aside: fire is energetic, whereas old age is associated with loss of energy. Might “blazing” be an extravagant or even ill-chosen image?

It would be ill-chosen if the clause required every property of fire to apply to an aging man. But a metaphor selects a relationship. Brightness, spread, and the change in appearance can matter without implying youthful vigor. Ibn ʿĀshūr develops the image through a shining appearance spreading across a dark surface. He also reads the physical descriptions as an appeal for mercy rather than information God needs to learn. [C19-05: commentary on 19:4–6](https://quran.com/19:4/tafsirs/arabic-tanweer-tafseer)

That last observation helps recover the sentence’s purpose. Zakariyyā is addressing the one to whom his condition is already known. The language presents his need within a relationship. One need not share the prayer’s theology to recognize this as its communicative situation.

On the reading offered here, the clause’s vigor makes the advance of age vivid. The loss of strength does not prevent the description from having force. Indeed, the contrast may intensify the presentation: the speaker is weakening while the visible signs of age seem active. This is an interpretive proposal. It should be tested against the surrounding passage, not presented as a hidden physical fact or a measured psychological effect.

There is also a difference between seeing and being told. “I am old” supplies a category. A description of weakness and whitened hair gives the reader particulars through which to imagine the predicament. The subsequent statement of confidence prevents the verse from ending with bodily decline. The prayer continues beyond what the body appears to permit.

This reading offers a reason to value the image besides its novelty. It contributes to the speaker’s position and the request that follows. If we removed it, the prayer would still contain aging and need, but one of its ways of making them present would disappear. That is a defensible account of contribution. It is not proof that no alternative could contribute equally well by different means.

The modern study of classical poetics can sharpen this distinction. Lara Harb’s publisher-provided summary of her chapter on *naẓm* describes sentence construction as capable of prompting discovery through implicit meaning and context. It situates Qur’anic and poetic beauty within a connected field of analysis. This is a useful research orientation, not an empirical finding about how every reader experiences 19:4. Only the chapter summary and bibliographic information were inspected for this draft. [C19-06: Harb, chapter 5](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108780483.007)

## Give the alternative explanation its strength

A skeptical reader may accept the entire interpretation and still say: this is what accomplished literature does. It makes grammar, imagery, and situation work together. Why should this example count against exceptional human authorship?

At this stage it does not decide between the explanations. A striking and well-integrated metaphor is compatible with human literary skill. It would be circular to define the effect as superhuman because it occurs in scripture and then use the effect to prove that the scripture is superhuman.

The fair response is to enlarge the investigation. Examine accomplished Arabic writing in context, including writing whose effects differ from the Qur’an’s. Give each passage an opportunity to succeed at its own purpose. A restrained account of aging may be excellent because it withholds the dramatic image this verse supplies. A poem may develop an image over many lines because its purpose differs from the compression of a prayer.

A comparison therefore needs two questions. How effectively does each work accomplish its purpose? And, where the purposes genuinely overlap, which differences in expression matter? Neither question is answered by counting metaphors or by penalizing another work for lacking the Qur’an’s exact features.

The strongest human-authorship account can accommodate exceptional achievement. It need not predict ordinary language, obvious flaws, or unevenness in every short passage. To challenge that account, later chapters must investigate sustained performance, complete compositions, historical evidence, and fair alternatives. Even then, literary conclusions and conclusions about origin require separate reasoning.

There is an equally important challenge to the favorable interpretation itself. Perhaps the sense of comprehensive grayness arises mainly from our prior knowledge that the speaker is old. Perhaps familiarity makes the original seem inevitable. Perhaps an unfamiliar reader would regard a different construction as clearer. These possibilities do not refute al-Jurjānī’s analysis in advance. They identify what an investigation would have to distinguish.

## What measurement could add

The comparison can generate researchable questions without turning interpretation into a fictitious score. One proposed study would ask proficient Arabic readers to judge several carefully reviewed versions of the sentence. It would separate at least two tasks: an inference about how extensive the grayness appears, and a judgment of how well the wording serves the prayer. The first asks about communicated meaning; the second asks about literary fitness.

A simple descriptive contrast would be:

**Δextent = mean(original ratings) − mean(alternative ratings)**

Here, each average would summarize readers’ ratings of perceived extent under a predefined scale, provided that treating its intervals as comparable is justified. Otherwise, the analysis should report ordered-category probabilities or paired preference proportions. A positive difference would mean that these readers, under these conditions, judged the original to suggest more pervasive grayness. It would not measure the percentage of an actual head that had whitened, and it would not establish divine authorship.

No such study has been conducted for this chapter. The equation specifies a possible observation; it reports no result.

To make the study informative, the versions would need grammatical review, randomized presentation, and controls drawn from accomplished human writing. Some alternatives should be intended as improvements. Recognition and prior familiarity must be recorded, since simply hiding the source label cannot make a famous verse anonymous. Presenting the clause alone and within its prayer would help investigate the contribution of context, although the precise design must avoid teaching participants the contrast before measuring it.

Readers may disagree systematically. Specialists might distinguish a construction that other readers scarcely notice. Religious commitment might correlate with judgments, or it might not. The data should show those possibilities instead of averaging them away. Repeated judgments from one person and repeated versions of one sentence cannot be treated as independent witnesses to a universal claim.

One especially useful outcome would be a division between interpretation and preference. Readers might agree that the original presents more comprehensive grayness while differing over whether that is desirable. Such a result would strengthen a linguistic account while leaving an aesthetic dispute open. Conversely, if context eliminates the difference between constructions, that would narrow the claim we should make for the grammar alone.

## The evidence we can carry forward

The example now yields something more definite than an invitation to admire Arabic. Its wording is available for inspection. The head is the grammatical subject of blazing. An established classical interpretation explains the final accusative as specifying grayness and connects the construction with pervasive spread. The original attribution to al-Jurjānī is verifiable. A reading of the whole verse relates its physical imagery to need, remembered confidence, and prayer.

These findings occupy different levels. The grammatical forms are observations. The account of their effect is an interpretation. Calling that effect well suited to the prayer is a judgment. An argument that revelation best explains the Qur’an’s achievement would have to incorporate this evidence alongside much more, including evidence that could count against it.

The affirmative case gains credibility when those levels remain visible. It can invite the reader to recognize an achievement without demanding an immediate verdict on origin. It can also learn from a reader who accepts the grammatical analysis but disputes the evaluation.

We have examined one clause within one prayer. The next step is to examine a complete composition, where individual choices must contribute to a whole. The relevant question will become harder and more useful: how do the parts work together, and what would a serious comparison have to preserve?

### Source and review note

Source identifiers refer to `research/sources-19-4.json`. Six source records were inspected at the scopes recorded there. Only the al-Jurjānī source was checked against its printed page images; the tafsīr sources are digital transcriptions. Harb is cited only for the available publisher summary, not as a claim to have inspected the full chapter. No reader experiment, comparative ranking, or comprehensive literature review is represented as completed. The proposed interpretation and the original working translations remain open to independent Arabic, literary, and editorial review.
